name: Cockburn Street
description: Cockburn Street was cut through the Old Town's solid tenement blocks between 1856 and 1864, curving from the High Street down to Market Street to ease the gradient for carriages heading to the new Waverley Station below. It was built by the High Street and Railway Station Access Company under the Railway Station Acts of 1853 and 1860. Most of its ornate buildings went up under architects Peddie & Kinnear, whose interlocking 'PK' monogram is still carved into stonework along the street today. It took its name from Henry, Lord Cockburn, an Edinburgh judge and early defender of the Old Town's character, who died in 1854 before construction began.
interesting_fact: Lord Cockburn never saw the street bearing his name, and the irony runs deeper: shortly before his death he'd campaigned loudly against Old Town 'improvement' schemes that swept away historic buildings much like the ones demolished to build this one. Its curving pavement is now known for independent shops selling records, comics, tattoos and vintage clothes, a countercultural reputation quite different from the grand retail parade its builders had in mind.

name: Craig's Close
description: One of the Old Town's oldest closes, named after John Craig, a burgess who acquired the land through marriage, Craig's Close was for two centuries a hub of Edinburgh printing. Andro Hart printed an influential Scottish edition of the Bible from a house at its head around 1610, and Edinburgh's first regular newspaper, the Edinburgh Courant, rolled off presses here from 14 February 1705. Its original High Street entrance, once almost directly opposite the Mercat Cross, was sealed off in 1932 when the council's municipal offices were extended; today the close survives only as a short, narrow passage between Cockburn Street and Market Street.
interesting_fact: A plaque near the foot of the close's steps commemorates poet Robert Fergusson's membership of the Cape Club, a boisterous eighteenth-century dining and drinking society for Edinburgh's writers and artists. Barely wide enough for two people to pass, the close is easy to miss entirely from Cockburn Street, yet across two centuries it printed some of the earliest scripture and news ever set in type in Scotland.

name: Old Fishmarket Close
description: Old Fishmarket Close plunges steeply from the High Street down to the Cowgate, named for a fish market once held partway down its length; its earliest recorded name, Swift's Wynd, dates back to 1427. During the 'Lang Siege' of 1573 the close was bombarded along with much of the Royal Mile, and in April 1585 a girl working here became the first recorded victim when plague reached Edinburgh. George Heriot, the goldsmith later famous for endowing George Heriot's School, lived in the close in 1586. In 1705 a Dutchman named Abraham Sever reportedly kept a touring elephant in a flat here, to the fury of a baker below whose ovens suffered from the animal's droppings.
interesting_fact: The close has been renamed repeatedly over the centuries: Home Close in 1707, Gourlay's Close in 1756, and Carmichael's Close in 1722, before finally settling on 'Old Fishmarket Close' for the market once held partway down its slope. A quirky cast-metal sign of leaping fish, in silver and bright pink, still swings above its High Street archway today, keeping the old market's memory alive long after the last stall closed.

name: Anchor Close
description: Recorded from 1714, Anchor Close took its name from a tavern that stood at its head, and it originally ran unbroken from the High Street down to Market Street until Cockburn Street was carved through the middle of it in the 1850s, splitting it in two. Its most notable resident was printer William Smellie, who ran his press from the close and produced the first edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica between 1768 and 1771, as well as the first Edinburgh-printed volume of Robert Burns's poems in 1787. Sir Walter Scott's parents lived in the close until 1771, not long before the novelist was born nearby.
interesting_fact: Smellie also founded the Crochallan Fencibles, a rowdy Edinburgh drinking club that met in a tavern in the close, taking its odd name from 'Crodh Chailein' (Colin's Cattle), a favourite song of the landlord, paired with 'Fencibles', the term for home-defence militia regiments. Robert Burns was introduced to the club by Smellie in 1787 and became a member, reportedly composing some of his bawdier verses purely for the group's private amusement.
source_notes: Smellie/Britannica printing history, Burns's 1787 Edinburgh edition, Walter Scott's parents and the Crochallan Fencibles corroborated across Canmore/trove.scot, Wikipedia's Crochallan Fencibles and William Smellie articles. name: Tron Kirk Market
description: The Tron Kirk's foundation stone was laid on 4 March 1637, commissioned by Charles I after St Giles' up the street became Edinburgh's cathedral and its displaced parish needed a church of its own. Designed by master mason John Mylne, blending Gothic tracery with Dutch-influenced classical detailing, it wasn't finished until the 1640s because of the Wars of the Covenant. Its original steeple was destroyed in the Great Fire of Edinburgh in 1824; the current spire, by R. & R. Dickson, replaced it in 1828. The congregation held its final service here in 1952, merging with St Giles'. The kirk's name comes from the tron, a weighing beam that stood outside until around 1800, taxing goods sold nearby.
interesting_fact: Restoration in the 1970s uncovered the cobbled surface of Marlin's Wynd beneath the floor, a paved street thought to be among the oldest in Scotland, named after mason Walter Merlioun who lived there around 1500; part remains visible under glass panels today. After decades as a heritage centre, the building reopened in July 2022 as Tron Kirk Market, run by the Scottish Design Exchange, where local makers sell jewellery, art and craft from stalls inside the old nave.

name: The Milkman
description: The Milkman occupies one of Cockburn Street's most photographed corners: a slender stone tower wedged onto a genuinely triangular plot near the foot of the street, its steeply pitched roof narrowing up to a single ornamental point. The shop itself is barely wider than its own doorway, its floor plan following the wedge of ground it sits on so tightly that there's room for little more than a till and a handful of customers. It's part of a Baronial-styled terrace built in 1859, when Cockburn Street was cut through the Old Town to give Waverley Station a direct route down from the High Street - its deliberate curve was designed to disguise the fact it slices diagonally across the medieval street pattern above it.
interesting_fact: Before it sold coffee, the building was a confectioner's - a hand-painted fascia sign uncovered during a 2016 restoration still reveals that former trade. Edinburgh World Heritage contributed more than £6,000 toward the project, which repaired the shop's original timber shutters (still slid into slots beneath the windows each night) and the antique lettering, carried out in partnership with shop owner Mark Donald.

name: Sir Chris Hoy Gold Post Box
description: This ordinary Victorian pillar box was painted gold in August 2012, one of two in Edinburgh honouring Sir Chris Hoy after his double gold-medal haul at the London Olympics - this one in Hunter Square marking his win in the men's keirin, with a second box on Hanover Street for his team sprint gold. Royal Mail repainted a post box gold in the hometown of every British Olympic and Paralympic gold medallist that summer, the first time in modern history the colour of the country's post boxes had ever changed from their traditional red.
interesting_fact: The gold paint job was meant to be temporary, quietly restored to red once the games ended - but the public reaction was so strong that Royal Mail made the change permanent that November, adding a small plaque naming the athlete and medal to every box. Hoy, born and raised in Edinburgh, won his second gold of the games in the team sprint days later, becoming Britain's most decorated Olympic cyclist and, within months, Sir Chris Hoy.
